etymology: From blameless + -ness. Renders the Greek amemptos, “blameless, faultless,” and amōmos, “without spot or blemish”; and the Hebrew tāmīm, “complete, sound, blameless.”
biblical_def: Blamelessness in Scripture is not sinless perfection—Scripture never claims that for any but Christ—but the practical, walk-and-conduct standing of a believer against whom no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained. The Hebrew tāmīm is the great Old Testament word: Noah was perfect (tāmīm) in his generations; Abraham was charged, walk before me, and be thou perfect; Job was perfect and upright; the priestly sacrifices were to be without blemish—the same word applied morally to persons. The Greek amemptos means literally “not to be blamed”: Paul commends the Philippians to be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation; Zacharias and Elisabeth were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless; Paul says of himself touching the righteousness which is in the law, he was blameless. The qualifications for elders and deacons in the Pastorals turn on this very category: a bishop then must be blameless; let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless. Blamelessness is therefore a real, achievable, expected standing of every mature believer and especially every officer of the church—not perfection, but the absence of any legitimate moral or doctrinal charge that can be sustained against him by a fair examination. It includes the open, walking-in-the-light life that has nothing to hide; the long, consistent pattern of conduct that gives no occasion for credible accusation; the integrity that aligns the inward and outward man; and the readiness, when accusation is made falsely, to bear it with the calm conscience of one who knows that the charge is not true. The eschatological promise gathers the doctrine to its consummation: that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish—the church Christ will at last present to Himself in the perfect blamelessness toward which the saint’s present sanctification is being shaped, by the Spirit, in his own life now.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BLAMELESS as without fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure; in scripture, the practical walk and conduct against which no legitimate charge can be sustained.
webster_full: BLAMELESS, a. — Without fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure. A bishop then must be blameless (1 Tim 3:2). 2. Free from imputation of fault; harmless; unblamable; as, to live a blameless life.
BLAMELESSNESS, n. — Innocence; a state of being not deserving of censure; the practical walk and conduct of one against whom no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained.
scriptures: Philippians 2:15
That ye may be blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world.
1 Timothy 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach.
Luke 1:6
And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless.
Ephesians 5:27
That he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish.
corruption_summary: Blamelessness is corrupted, on one side, by the perfectionist register that treats it as sinless perfection unattainable in this life and so quietly drops the standard altogether—and on the other by the laxist register that has so lowered the bar for officers and members that the New Testament’s blameless qualifications are no longer practically applied.
corruption_paragraphs: The perfectionist corruption confuses blamelessness with sinless perfection and so concludes that the standard cannot be met in this life and need not be pressed in pastoral practice. Scripture refuses the confusion. Zacharias and Elisabeth were blameless, yet Zacharias was struck dumb for unbelief moments after his blamelessness was named—the category is real, the perfection is not yet. Paul names himself blameless touching the law’s righteousness and elsewhere counts that righteousness as dung. The two stand together. Blamelessness is the practical walk-and-conduct standing of one against whom no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained; it is real, achievable, and expected of mature believers and especially of officers; it is not sinless perfection, which awaits the resurrection. Recover the distinction, and the standard returns to its proper pastoral use: not as an impossible counsel of perfection but as the real, examinable walk Scripture commands and the church is to require of those it sets in office.

The opposite and more contemporary corruption is the laxist register that has so lowered the bar for officers and members that the New Testament’s blameless qualifications are no longer practically applied. Elders are ordained whose lives are known to bear credible moral charges; deacons are appointed without serious examination; the very category of a scandalous Christian—one whose life gives such occasion for credible accusation that his name itself is a stumbling-block to the gospel—is treated indulgently rather than addressed. Scripture is sharper. A bishop then must be blameless—the requirement is given because the office requires it, because the church’s credibility before the watching world depends in part upon it, and because the saint’s own walk is built up or torn down by the patterns of conduct his shepherds embody. Recover the standard. Examine those proposed for office, address scandalous patterns through the discipline Scripture appoints, and aim the whole body toward the blamelessness Paul commands as the practical fruit of the gospel: blameless and harmless, the sons of God, without rebuke, in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation.
roots_summary: Greek amemptos (not to be blamed) and amōmos (without spot or blemish); Hebrew tāmīm (complete, sound, blameless)—the practical walk-and-conduct standing against which no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained.
roots_lines: Greek amemptos (G273) — blameless, faultless (Phil 2:15; Luke 1:6; 1 Thess 3:13).
Greek amōmos (G299) — without spot or blemish (Eph 1:4; 5:27; Heb 9:14; Jude 24).
Greek anepilemptos (G423) — not to be laid hold of, irreproachable (1 Tim 3:2 of bishops).
Hebrew tāmīm (H8549) — complete, sound, blameless (Gen 6:9; 17:1; Job 1:1; Ps 15:2).
usage: Blamelessness is not sinless perfection but the practical walk against which no legitimate moral or doctrinal charge can be sustained.
A bishop then must be blameless—the requirement is given because the office requires it and the church’s credibility depends in part upon it.
Perfectionist confusion drops the standard as unattainable; laxist confusion drops it as inconvenient; biblical blamelessness is real, examinable, and expected of mature believers.

etymology: From sweet + -ness. Renders the Hebrew māthōq, “sweet,” and the imagery of honey, the honeycomb, and the rock-of-honey throughout the Psalms; and the Greek glukuōs, “sweet.”
biblical_def: Sweetness in Scripture is one of the most surprising and tender categories used for the Word of God, the LORD Himself, and the experiences of grace by the saint. The Psalmist’s great line sets the keynote: how sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth; and again: more to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb; and in the great Psalm 119: I have rejoiced in the way of thy testimonies, as much as in all riches. The Word is not merely true, not merely authoritative, not merely necessary—though it is all of these—but sweet, with the deep palatable sweetness that the saint comes to taste with an inward palate the natural man does not possess. Peter sets the same imagery at the start of the Christian life: as newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious. The taste of the LORD’s graciousness is the entry-point of the maturing Christian appetite. Psalm 34 makes the invitation universal: O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him. The category extends to the experiences of grace themselves: the sweetness of answered prayer, the sweetness of pardoned sin, the sweetness of communion with God in the closet, the sweetness of the Lord’s Supper, the sweetness of the gathered saints in worship. Even tribulation, says the Puritan tradition rightly tracing the biblical pattern, has its sweetness for the saint who has tasted the LORD’s comforts in it: it is good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes. The pastoral application is double. First, the saint is invited to taste—to come to the Word, the LORD, the sacraments, the means of grace with an expectant inward palate and to develop the capacity to taste their sweetness. Second, the absence of any sense of sweetness in the things of God is the most ominous spiritual diagnostic Scripture supplies: the soul that has lost the sweetness of the Word is in danger; the soul that has never had it has not yet tasted that the Lord is gracious; and the soul awakened to the sweetness is the soul that has begun to live the regenerate life as God means it to be lived.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SWEETNESS as the quality of being sweet, in any of its senses; pleasing taste; agreeableness; melody; figuratively, gentleness; mildness; amiableness; in scripture, the deep palatable sweetness of God’s Word and presence to the regenerate soul.
webster_full: SWEETNESS, n. — 1. The quality of being sweet, in any of its senses; as, the sweetness of fruit; the sweetness of perfumes. 2. Agreeableness of taste; that taste which gives pleasure. 3. Agreeableness; pleasing quality; as, the sweetness of disposition or temper. 4. Melody; pleasing harmony; as, the sweetness of music. 5. In scripture, the deep palatable sweetness of God’s Word and presence to the regenerate soul (Psa 19:10; 119:103).
scriptures: Psalm 119:103
How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!
Psalm 19:10
More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold: sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb.
Psalm 34:8
O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.
1 Peter 2:2-3
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby: If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.
corruption_summary: The sweetness of God’s Word and presence is corrupted by the dry, dutiful register of the believer who reads Scripture as obligation without any expectation of tasted sweetness—and by the inverse mistake of seeking subjective emotional sweetness in worship and prayer apart from the substantive Word and presence that alone produce the biblical kind.
corruption_paragraphs: The dry, dutiful register is the most common contemporary corruption of biblical sweetness. The believer reads his Scripture as obligation, attends his services as discipline, prays his prayers as duty, all without any expectation that the Word will be sweet to his taste, that the LORD’s graciousness will be a tasted reality, or that the means of grace will produce in him the deep palatable enjoyment Scripture describes. The Psalmist who said how sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth would not recognize the inward palate of the contemporary dutiful believer, who has the doctrine of the Word’s authority but has lost the experience of its sweetness. Recover the doctrine and the expectation, and the appetite revives: come to Scripture with the inward palate ready to taste, ask the LORD to set the sweetness of His Word upon the soul, return to the texts that have once tasted sweet, and watch the inward palate awaken to the food God has prepared for it.

The opposite corruption is the seeking of subjective emotional sweetness in worship and prayer apart from the substantive Word and presence that alone produce the biblical kind. The believer chases the feeling-of-sweetness through music, atmosphere, and engineered experience, and identifies the engineered lift with the biblical sweetness that is in fact wrought by the gospel itself. The two are not the same. Biblical sweetness is the inward palate’s response to the actual substance of God’s Word and presence; engineered emotional lift is a separate thing that may accompany worship but is not itself the sweetness of which Scripture speaks. Recover both ends: come to the Word and the LORD expecting tasted sweetness as a real, experiential reality (against the dry corruption), and seek that sweetness in the actual substance of the Word and presence and not in engineered feeling (against the inverse corruption). The inward palate is real; the food is real; the sweetness is real; the believer’s discipline is to come to the table where it is served.
roots_summary: Hebrew māthōq (sweet) and the imagery of honey, honeycomb, and the rock-of-honey throughout the Psalms; Greek glukuōs (sweet)—the deep palatable sweetness of God’s Word and presence to the regenerate inward palate.
roots_lines: Hebrew māthōq (H4966) — sweet, pleasant (Prov 16:24; 24:13; Eccl 11:7; Ezek 3:3).
Hebrew māthaōq (H4985) — to be sweet, become sweet.
Hebrew d’vāsh (H1706) — honey (the sweetness comparison standard).
Greek glukuōs (G1099) — sweet (Rev 10:9-10, the bitter-sweet scroll).
usage: How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!—the inward palate’s response to the substance of God’s Word.
O taste and see that the LORD is good—the LORD’s graciousness is itself a tasted reality, not merely an inferred one.
Dry duty has lost the sweetness; engineered emotionalism substitutes a different feeling for it; biblical sweetness is the inward palate’s real response to real substance.

etymology: From weary + -ness; weary from Old English wērig, “tired, exhausted.” Renders the Hebrew yāga, “to be weary, work hard,” and the Greek kopos, “labor to weariness,” and ekluō, “to faint, grow weary.”
biblical_def: Weariness in Scripture is the real, often-honored, sometimes-warned-against fatigue of soul or body that comes from sustained labor, prolonged suffering, hard providences, persistent sin, or the long discouragement of waiting. The Bible does not pretend the saint will be exempt; it teaches him both how to bear the weariness rightly and how to recover from it. Christ Himself, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well at Sychar; the Christ in whom dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily was a man who could be tired by the road. Paul is candid about his ministerial weariness: in weariness and painfulness, in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, in fastings often, in cold and nakedness. The prophets weary themselves in pleading; the saints weary themselves in waiting; the soul wearies itself in sin (thou art wearied in the greatness of thy way, says the LORD to apostate Israel); the body wearies under the sun, the curse, and the years. Against all weariness Scripture presses promises and disciplines. The promise to those who wait: but they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint. The promise to those who labor in the gospel: let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. The promise to those who endure: consider him that endured such contradiction of sinners against himself, lest ye be wearied and faint in your minds. The Christ who came down from heaven to make atonement makes also the offer to the weary themselves: come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. Weariness is therefore real, honored when borne in the Lord’s work, warned against when it tempts toward faintness in well-doing, and answered by the rest Christ offers—a rest that is not the absence of all labor but the deeper rest of the soul taking its load upon Him and finding His yoke easy and His burden light.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WEARINESS as the state of being weary; lassitude or exhaustion of strength or feeling, induced by labor; fatigue; tedium; in scripture, the real fatigue of soul or body that meets the saint in the Lord’s service and waits to be answered by His promised rest.
webster_full: WEARINESS, n. — 1. The state of being weary; that lassitude or exhaustion of strength which is induced by labor; fatigue; tedium. 2. The state of being affected with feelings of disgust at being detained too long. 3. In scripture, the real fatigue of soul or body that comes from sustained labor, prolonged suffering, or hard providence—to be borne in the Lord’s strength and answered by the rest Christ offers.
WEARY, a. — 1. Having the strength exhausted by toil or exertion; tired; fatigued. 2. Having the patience exhausted, or the mind yielding to discouragement.
scriptures: Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Galatians 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
Matthew 11:28-29
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls.
John 4:6
Now Jacob’s well was there. Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour.
corruption_summary: Weariness is corrupted, on one side, by the comfort-and-self-care register of the present age that treats every weariness as a problem to be eliminated rather than a real fatigue to be borne in the Lord and answered by His rest—and on the other by the flesh-driven workaholism that despises weariness as weakness and ignores Christ’s own invitation to the weary.
corruption_paragraphs: The comfort-and-self-care register of the present age treats every weariness as a problem to be eliminated by better boundaries, more self-care, and reduced commitment. Scripture acknowledges weariness as a real fatigue of soul and body, sometimes honored (Paul’s ministerial weariness), sometimes warned against (the temptation to faint in well-doing), and always to be borne in the Lord’s strength and answered by the promised rest. The reflexive contemporary instinct to reduce commitments at the first sign of fatigue can produce a Christianity that has never strained itself in the Lord’s service and so has never had the occasion to prove the strength He promises to those who wait on Him. The biblical disposition is different: when the weariness comes, it is borne, brought to the Lord, set against the eschatological harvest (in due season we shall reap, if we faint not), and answered by the rest of the One who Himself was wearied on the way and who promises rest to all who come to Him with their load.

The opposite corruption is the flesh-driven workaholism that despises weariness as weakness and ignores Christ’s own invitation to the weary. The minister or saint who treats fatigue as failure, who refuses to come to the Lord with his load, who runs in his own strength without ever taking up the easy yoke and the light burden, eventually finds either burnout or embittered exhaustion at the end of his striving. Christ’s invitation is not optional. Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. The weary saint is to come; the weary minister is to come; the load is to be brought to the One who has invited the bringing; the yoke is to be exchanged for the easier one; and the rest is to be received not as the absence of all labor but as the deeper rest of the soul resting in the strength of its Lord. Recover both ends: refuse the comfort culture’s premature retreat from sustained service, and refuse the flesh-driven workaholism that scorns the weariness Christ invites the weary to bring.
roots_summary: Hebrew yāga (to be weary, work hard) and lā’āh (to be weary); Greek kopos (labor to weariness) and ekluō (to faint, grow weary)—the real fatigue of soul or body, borne in the Lord and answered by His promised rest.
roots_lines: Hebrew yāga (H3021) — to be weary, work hard.
Hebrew lā’āh (H3811) — to be weary, exhausted (Isa 1:14; Jer 6:11).
Greek kopos (G2873) — labor, toil, weariness (2 Cor 11:27).
Greek ekluō (G1590) — to be loosed out, faint, grow weary (Gal 6:9; Heb 12:3, 5).
usage: They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength... they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint—the promise to those who wait.
Let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not—the warning to those who serve.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest—Christ’s invitation to the weary themselves.

etymology: From Old French destresse, “narrowness, anguish,” from Latin distringere, “to draw apart, hinder.” Renders the Hebrew tsarāh, “narrowness, distress,” from tsar (narrow), and the Greek thlipsis, “pressure, affliction.”
biblical_def: Distress in Scripture is the soul’s tight, pressed-in condition under affliction—the narrow place from which the saint cries to the LORD and out of which the LORD characteristically delivers His people. The Hebrew imagery is geometric: tsarāh from tsar (narrow) pictures the saint constricted, hemmed in, with no room to maneuver. The Greek thlipsis picks up the same image: pressure, tribulation, the inward squeeze of outward affliction. The Psalter is saturated with the verb-pair of distress and deliverance: I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place; then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he saved them out of their distresses (a refrain repeated four times in Ps 107); thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Paul gathers the same theology under the New Testament: who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?... Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. The biblical pattern of distress has therefore four marks. First, it is real: Scripture does not pretend the saint will be exempt from the tight places, the constricting providences, the pressure that bears in on body and soul. Second, it is the appointed setting in which the soul’s cry rises and the LORD’s deliverance is wrought: before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word; the very narrowness of the distress is the setting in which God’s salvation is most vividly known. Third, it does not separate the saint from the love of Christ; the apostle’s comprehensive list (Rom 8:35) is given precisely to show that no distress, however severe, can cut the bond. Fourth, it is the present antechamber to glory: I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us; and Christ’s own promise in John 16:33: in the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world. The biblical disposition under distress is therefore neither denial nor despair but the cry of the saint who knows the LORD’s habit—and waits, even in the narrowest place, for the deliverance the LORD characteristically works for those who call upon Him.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DISTRESS as extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; severe affliction; calamity; the act of distraining; in scripture, the constricted condition of the soul under affliction, set against the LORD’s characteristic deliverance.
webster_full: DISTRESS, n. — 1. The act of distraining; the taking of any personal chattel from a wrong-doer, to procure satisfaction. 2. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind. 3. The cause of pain or anguish; affliction; calamity. 4. A state of danger or extreme need, in which we have no resource. I will save them from all their distresses (Ezek 37:23).
DISTRESSED, pp. or a. — Suffering great pain or torture; harassed; afflicted with calamity; oppressed with want.
scriptures: Psalm 120:1
In my distress I cried unto the LORD, and he heard me.
Psalm 107:6
Then they cried unto the LORD in their trouble, and he delivered them out of their distresses.
Romans 8:35
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
John 16:33
These things I have spoken unto you, that in me ye might have peace. In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.
corruption_summary: Distress is corrupted, on one side, by the prosperity-and-comfort register that treats every tight place as evidence of God’s absence or the saint’s insufficient faith—and on the other by the stoic register that minimizes distress as unworthy of expression, against the Psalter’s candid cries and Christ’s own tears.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity-and-comfort register reads every distress as evidence of God’s absence or the saint’s insufficient faith—the believer is told that the LORD wants him in the large place, never in the narrow, and that the persistence of distress in his life means something is wrong with his praying, his believing, or his obedience. Scripture refuses the reading. The Psalter is saturated with distress; the apostle’s catalog in 2 Corinthians 11 lists his own distresses at length; Christ Himself in Gethsemane was exceeding sorrowful, even unto death; the saints of Hebrews 11 were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, slain with the sword. Distress is the regular setting of the Christian life in this present age, and the LORD’s characteristic deliverance is wrought precisely in and through the distress, not by exempting the saint from it. Recover the doctrine, and the saint stops reading every tight place as evidence of divine displeasure and begins reading it as the appointed antechamber in which the cry rises and the deliverance is wrought.

The opposite corruption is the stoic register that minimizes distress as unworthy of expression, requires the saint to perform a composure he does not feel, and reads the Psalmist’s tearful complaints as a lower spirituality the mature believer has transcended. The Psalter and Christ’s own example refuse this. The Psalmist cries, complains, weeps, asks how long?—and the Spirit included his complaint in the inspired hymnal of the church. Christ wept at Lazarus’s tomb, sweat as it were great drops of blood in Gethsemane, cried with a loud voice on the cross. The expression of distress before God is biblically authorized; the suppression of it as a token of strength is not the higher spirituality but a lower one. Recover both ends. Refuse the prosperity reading that treats distress as evidence of divine absence, and refuse the stoic reading that requires its suppression—and the saint can bring his actual distress to the actual LORD who has the actual habit of delivering His people out of their distresses, characteristically in His time and in His way.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsarāh (narrowness, distress) from tsar (narrow); Greek thlipsis (pressure, affliction)—the soul’s tight, pressed-in condition under affliction, set against the LORD’s characteristic deliverance and the love of Christ from which it cannot separate the saint.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsarāh (H6869) — distress, trouble (the “narrowness” word; Ps 9:9; 22:11; 50:15; 119:143).
Hebrew tsar (H6862) — narrow, tight; the geometric root of distress imagery.
Greek thlipsis (G2347) — pressure, affliction, tribulation (the great NT distress word).
Greek stenōchōria (G4730) — narrowness of place, anguish (Rom 8:35; 2 Cor 6:4).
usage: I called upon the LORD in distress: the LORD answered me, and set me in a large place—the saint’s characteristic experience and the LORD’s characteristic answer.
Distress is the appointed antechamber in which the soul’s cry rises and the LORD’s salvation is most vividly known.
Prosperity reading treats distress as divine absence; stoic reading treats it as unworthy of expression; biblical pattern brings the actual distress to the actual LORD who actually delivers.

etymology: Latin terror, “great fear, dread,” from terrere (to frighten). Renders the Hebrew émāh, “dread, terror,” and the Greek phobos, “fear, terror,” especially in its objective sense of that-which-is-to-be-feared.
biblical_def: Terror in Scripture has two distinct biblical registers, and the contemporary believer often hears only one. The terror of the LORD is the apostolic name for the awe-evoking, judgment-shaped reality of the holy God Himself, set forth as the proper motive of evangelistic urgency: knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men. Paul does not name this terror to embarrass the gospel but to anchor its urgency: the holy God who will judge the world in righteousness through Christ is no less holy and no less judging because His mercy is wide; the terror of being on the wrong side of His day is real, and the apostle’s persuasion of men is grounded partly in that terror as well as in the love of Christ that compels him. The Old Testament prophets uniformly speak of the LORD’s terror as His characteristic effect upon the unrepentant: the day of the LORD cometh, cruel both with wrath and fierce anger... and they shall be afraid: pangs and sorrows shall take hold of them. The second register is the fear of terror the saint is to refuse: be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; fear not their fear, neither be afraid; the threats of the world’s power, the intimidations of the persecutor, the dread-inducing pressures of the spirit of the age are not to terrify the saint who has set apart the Lord God in his heart. Peter explicitly weaves the two: Sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear: Having a good conscience. The biblical doctrine therefore holds two terrors in their proper places: the terror of the LORD, which is the gospel-grounded urgency motive of evangelism and the personal awe that becomes the regenerate soul before its holy Maker; and the terror-of-men, which is the world’s attempt to intimidate the saint into silence and unfaithfulness, and which the saint refuses precisely because his heart has been sanctified by the greater terror of God. Where the contemporary church has lost the doctrine of God’s holiness and judgment, the first terror has shrunk to nothing; where the contemporary church has compromised before cultural pressure, the second terror has grown to occupy the space the first ought to fill. The recovery is to restore the proper proportions: terror of God, and the freedom from terror of man that the first terror produces.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TERROR as extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind; that which excites dread; in scripture, both the awe-evoking reality of the holy God Himself and the world’s threats which the saint is commanded not to fear.
webster_full: TERROR, n. — 1. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind. 2. That which excites dread; the cause of extreme fear. Rulers are not a terror to good works, but to the evil (Rom 13:3). 3. In scripture, the awe-evoking reality of the holy God Himself, as in the terror of the Lord (2 Cor 5:11).
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 5:11
Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.
Isaiah 8:12-13
Neither fear ye their fear, nor be afraid. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread.
But and if ye suffer for righteousness’ sake, happy are ye: and be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts...
Hebrews 10:31
It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
corruption_summary: Terror is corrupted, in the contemporary church, by the loss of the doctrine of God’s holiness and judgment that has shrunk the first terror (the terror of the Lord) to nothing—and by the cultural pressure that has grown the second terror (the fear of man) to occupy the space the first ought to fill, producing a Christianity that fears the world’s disapproval and does not fear the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The first terror—the terror of the Lord that Paul names as part of the motive of his evangelism—has shrunk to nearly nothing in much of the contemporary church. The doctrine of God’s holiness has been muted; the doctrine of God’s judgment has been quietly retired or eschatologically postponed beyond practical reach; the diagnostic seriousness of it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God has been domesticated into something gentler. The result is a Christianity in which no one is persuaded, in part, by the terror of the Lord—because the terror has been theologically defanged. Recover the doctrine of God’s holiness and judgment, recover the apostolic candor about the terror that motivates persuasion, and the gospel recovers its urgency and the saint his proper awe before the holy God whose mercy he has tasted.

The second terror has grown to fill the space the first ought to occupy. The contemporary believer often fears the world’s disapproval intensely (the social-media pile-on, the cancellation, the cultural marginalization, the loss of employment or platform for confessing biblical truth) and fears the LORD’s displeasure mildly or not at all. The apostles and prophets reverse the proportions. Sanctify the LORD of hosts himself; and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. Be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled. The greater terror frees the soul from the lesser: the saint who is rightly awed by the holy God can stand calmly before the world’s threats; the saint who fears the world and does not fear the LORD has reversed the proportions and will compromise wherever the world’s pressure exceeds the LORD’s felt weight. Recover the proper proportions, and the courage of confession returns, the freedom of speech returns, the steadiness of the faithful witness returns—all of it the proper fruit of the first terror sanctifying the heart and crowding the second terror out.
roots_summary: Hebrew émāh (dread, terror) and pachad (dread); Greek phobos (fear, terror, both subjective fear and the objective thing-feared)—the two biblical terrors held in proper proportion: terror of God, and the freedom from terror of man that the first terror produces.
roots_lines: Hebrew émāh (H367) — dread, terror (Gen 15:12; Ex 15:16; 23:27).
Hebrew pachad (H6343) — dread, terror (the “dread of the LORD” word).
Greek phobos (G5401) — fear, terror; both subjective fear and the objective thing-feared (2 Cor 5:11; 1 Pet 3:14).
Greek ekphobos (G1630) — very afraid, terrified (Heb 12:21, Moses at Sinai).
usage: Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men—Paul anchors evangelistic urgency in the apostolic candor about God’s holiness and judgment.
Be not afraid of their terror, neither be troubled; But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts—the greater terror frees the saint from the lesser.
Contemporary church has shrunk the first terror and grown the second; recovery is to restore the proper proportions—terror of God, freedom from terror of man.

etymology: Latin indignatio, “displeasure at what is unworthy,” from indignus (unworthy). Renders the Hebrew za‘am, “denunciation, indignation,” and the Greek aganaktēsis, “indignation,” and orge, “wrath,” in some uses.
biblical_def: Indignation in Scripture is the burning displeasure of a holy mind at what is unworthy of God—at sin, at injustice, at the desecration of holy things, at the oppression of the weak, at every act that ought not to be. It belongs first to God, who is constantly named as indignant against iniquity and oppression; and it belongs derivatively to the regenerate saint, whose conformity to Christ includes a Spirit-wrought indignation at the very things God Himself is indignant against. Christ’s own indignation is on display in the Gospels. He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts; He was much displeased (the Greek is éganaktēsen, indignant) when the disciples kept the children from Him; He twice cleared the temple of the merchants with a zeal-driven indignation; He pronounced repeated woes upon the scribes and Pharisees whose religion oppressed the people. Paul commends the Corinthians for the Spirit-wrought indignation their repentance produced: for behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!—naming indignation as one of the seven marks of true repentance toward sin. The prophets are saturated with the holy indignation of the LORD at oppression, idolatry, and the perversion of justice; the Psalms cry out for indignation against the workers of iniquity and the enemies of God’s people; Revelation announces the final indignation that will pour out upon all unrighteousness at the day of the Lord. The biblical doctrine is therefore that holy indignation is a virtue, not a vice—but a virtue requiring the most careful guarding because it lies adjacent to its corruptions: personal anger that is merely fleshly resentment dressed in religious language, faction-driven outrage that has lost the calm clarity of God-shaped displeasure, and self-righteous indignation that condemns in others what it indulges in itself. The Christ-shaped indignation is grieved before it is angry, is directed at what God is indignant against and not at personal slights, is patient with the sinner even when sharp with the sin, and yields itself to the LORD’s appointed channels of address (church discipline, civil-authority appeal, prophetic speech) rather than venting itself in the flesh.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines INDIGNATION as anger or extreme anger, mingled with contempt, disgust or abhorrence; the wrath of God; in scripture, the holy displeasure of a regenerate mind at what is unworthy of God.
webster_full: INDIGNATION, n. — 1. Anger or extreme anger, mingled with contempt, disgust or abhorrence. 2. The anger of a superior; extreme anger; particularly, the wrath of God against sinful men for their ingratitude and rebellion. 3. The effects of anger; the dreadful effects of God’s wrath; terrible judgments.
INDIGNANT, a. — Affected at once with anger and disdain; feeling the mingled emotions of wrath and scorn or contempt.
scriptures: Mark 3:5
And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand...
Mark 10:14
But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
2 Corinthians 7:11
For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear...
Psalm 7:11
God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day.
corruption_summary: Indignation is corrupted, on one side, by the therapeutic register that has trained the believer to suppress all righteous anger as toxic—and on the other by the online-outrage register that performs indignation chronically and at low cost, often venting personal resentment under the cover of moral seriousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic suppression of indignation is the more recent contemporary corruption. The believer is taught that all anger is unhealthy, that righteous indignation is a contradiction in terms, and that the mature soul has transcended the very capacity for the displeasure Scripture commends as a mark of true repentance and a likeness to Christ. The text refuses this. Christ Himself was angry at the Pharisees’ hardness, displeased with the disciples’ obstruction of the children, indignant at the temple’s desecration; Paul lists indignation among the seven marks of godly sorrow that worketh repentance; the Psalms and Prophets are saturated with the LORD’s indignation at oppression and idolatry. To suppress all indignation is not Christian maturity; it is the loss of a Spirit-wrought disposition Scripture itself commends. Recover the doctrine, and the saint regains the capacity to be properly grieved and properly angry at what God Himself is grieved and angry about—and the moral seriousness the gospel produces returns to the regenerate soul.

The opposite corruption is the online-outrage register that performs indignation chronically and at low cost. The believer scrolls his feeds, identifies the issue of the day, posts the requisite indignant response, and feels he has done his part—often without any of the carefulness, fear, vehement desire, zeal, or revenge (against the sin in himself first) that Paul names as the proper concomitants of biblical indignation. The performance is cheap; the substance is missing; and the recurring practice trains the soul into a chronic outrage that wears the dress of moral seriousness but is often closer to personal resentment, faction-loyalty, or sheer habit. Recover the Christ-shaped pattern: indignation that is grieved before it is angry, directed at what God is indignant against, patient with the sinner even when sharp with the sin, yielded to the LORD’s appointed channels of address. Indignation rightly held is a virtue; indignation chronically performed online and never patiently embodied is the cheap counterfeit.
roots_summary: Hebrew za‘am (denunciation, indignation) and chemah (heat, wrath); Greek aganaktēsis (indignation) and orgē (settled wrath)—the holy displeasure of God at sin and oppression, and the Spirit-wrought derivative displeasure of the regenerate soul at what God Himself opposes.
roots_lines: Hebrew za‘am (H2195) — denunciation, indignation, anger.
Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, wrath, indignation.
Greek aganakteō (G23) — to be indignant (Mark 10:14; 14:4; Matt 20:24; 21:15; 26:8; Luke 13:14).
Greek aganaktēsis (G24) — indignation (2 Cor 7:11).
usage: Christ’s own indignation in the Gospels (the temple, the hardness of hearts, the obstruction of the children) shows the Spirit-wrought displeasure as a Christ-likeness, not a sin.
What indignation—Paul names indignation as one of the seven marks of godly sorrow that worketh repentance.
Therapeutic suppression empties the category; online-outrage performance counterfeits it; biblical indignation is Christ-shaped, patient, and yielded to the LORD’s appointed channels.

etymology: From shamefaced (originally shamefast, “held fast by shame”) + -ness. The 1611 KJV translators rendered the Greek aidōs as shamefacedness in 1 Timothy 2:9—the deep, inward sense of modesty that knows what would be shameful and naturally inclines away from it.
biblical_def: Shamefacedness, in the King James Bible, renders the Greek aidōs—the deep, inward sense of modesty that has a healthy awareness of what would be shameful and naturally inclines the soul away from it. Paul commands it of Christian women in 1 Timothy 2:9: in like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array. The word is paired with sobriety (the cousin virtue of self-controlled soundness of mind) as the inner disposition that produces modest outward adornment, with the negative counterpart spelled out: not the conspicuous display of hair-art, jewelry, gold, and costly clothing that announces the wearer’s status, wealth, or sexual self-presentation. The deeper biblical category, however, extends beyond apparel. Shamefacedness is the regenerate soul’s inward sensitivity to what is shameful: the modesty that does not want to be exposed in immodest ways, the sensitivity that knows what ought to remain private, the reverence that does not want to display before God or men what God has called the saint to keep covered. In a fallen world, the loss of shamefacedness is one of the most diagnostic spiritual symptoms: where shame has been removed from what God has called shameful (the public display of nakedness, the exhibition of perversion, the boasting in what ought to be wept over, the parading of intimate matters before a watching audience), the soul has lost an inward register essential to its protection. Conversely, the recovery of shamefacedness is one of the surest marks of regenerate life: the new heart has been given an inward sensitivity to sin that the old heart did not possess, and the believer finds himself wanting to cover what he once would have displayed, to keep private what he once would have boasted, to flee from what he once would have pursued. The Pauline doctrine is therefore that shamefacedness is no relic of repressive culture but the proper interior disposition of a regenerate soul living modestly before God and others in a world that has, by the curse, much to be ashamed of, and much grace by which the redeemed are clothed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SHAMEFACED as bashful; easily confused or put out of countenance; modest; in scripture, the deep inward modesty that knows what would be shameful and inclines the soul away from it.
webster_full: SHAMEFACED, a. — Bashful; easily confused or put out of countenance; modest. In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety (1 Tim 2:9).
SHAMEFACEDNESS, n. — Bashfulness; excess of modesty; the inward sense of modesty that becomes a regenerate person, especially in apparel and bearing.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 2:9-10

In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array; But (which becometh women professing godliness) with good works.
1 Peter 3:3-4

Whose adorning let it not be that outward adorning of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel; But let it be the hidden man of the heart, in that which is not corruptible, even the ornament of a meek and quiet spirit, which is in the sight of God of great price.
Proverbs 11:22
As a jewel of gold in a swine’s snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.
Romans 1:27
And likewise also the men, leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their lust one toward another; men with men working that which is unseemly...
corruption_summary: Shamefacedness is corrupted, in the present age, by the systematic removal of shame from what God has called shameful (the public exhibition of nakedness, the celebration of perversion, the parading of intimate matters before watching audiences)—and by the inverse corruption in some traditions of attaching shame to ordinary bodily realities God has not called shameful, producing a brittle puritanism rather than the deep Christian modesty Scripture commends.
corruption_paragraphs: The systematic removal of shame from what God has called shameful is the most visible and most pastorally damaging contemporary corruption. The public exhibition of nakedness has become unremarkable in entertainment, advertising, and increasingly in daily life; the celebration of perversion has been institutionally normalized; the parading of intimate matters before watching audiences (social media, reality television, the public exhibition of relationships, sexuality, mental life) has trained a generation out of the inward sensitivity Scripture calls shamefacedness. The believer who absorbs the surrounding register loses, often unconsciously, the regenerate disposition that wants to cover what God has called shameful and to keep private what God has called private. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers also the inward register: a modesty in apparel, in speech, in the publication of his life, in what he watches and reads and admits to his eye—not as repression of the body or the affections, but as the proper deference of a creature living before the holy God in a world where much is shameful and much grace is given by which the redeemed are clothed.

The opposite corruption is the brittle puritanism that attaches shame to ordinary bodily realities God has not called shameful. The body itself is not shameful; sexuality within marriage is not shameful; the proper enjoyment of God’s creation is not shameful. Where a tradition has attached shame to these, it has produced a distortion of biblical shamefacedness that confuses the saint, oppresses the conscience with imaginary obligations, and often produces the very secret indulgences the over-shaming was meant to prevent. The biblical balance is precise. Shame attaches to what God has called shameful (sin, the public display of nakedness outside its proper marital context, the celebration of perversion, the boasting in what ought to be wept over); shame does not attach to what God has called good (the body itself, marital intimacy, the proper enjoyment of food, drink, beauty, and play within His ordinances). Recover both ends, and shamefacedness recovers its biblical shape: a deep inward modesty that knows what God has called shameful and inclines the soul away from it, paired with a confident enjoyment of what God has called good and a refusal to be shamed by what He has not.
roots_summary: Greek aidōs (modesty, shamefacedness—1 Tim 2:9; Heb 12:28); cousin Greek aischunē (shame); Hebrew bōsh (to be ashamed) and kelimmāh (shame)—the deep inward sensitivity to what is shameful that inclines the regenerate soul to modesty in apparel, speech, and self-publication.
roots_lines: Greek aidōs (G127) — modesty, shamefacedness, reverence (1 Tim 2:9; Heb 12:28).
Greek aischunē (G152) — shame (the cousin word for the felt experience of being shamed).
Hebrew bōsh (H954) — to be ashamed, put to shame.
Hebrew kelimmāh (H3639) — shame, disgrace.
usage: That women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety—the inward disposition producing the outward modesty.
Shamefacedness is the regenerate soul’s inward sensitivity to what God has called shameful, paired with the confident enjoyment of what He has called good.
The systematic removal of shame from what God has called shameful is the more visible contemporary corruption; brittle puritanism that attaches shame to what He has not is the inverse.

etymology: From empty + -ness; empty from Old English æmtig (leisure, vacancy). Renders the Hebrew hebel, “vapor, breath, vanity” (Ecclesiastes’ great keyword), and the Greek kenosis-family of words, “an emptying.”
biblical_def: Emptiness in Scripture is a category that runs in two directions, the diagnostic and the doctrinal—and the most surprising of the two is the doctrinal one. Diagnostically, the Bible names the emptiness of created things apart from God as the deep verdict of the Preacher of Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity. The Hebrew hebel means literally vapor, breath—the visible exhalation on a winter morning, present for a moment and then gone. The Preacher applies this verdict to wealth, pleasure, wisdom, work, fame, even life itself when considered apart from God: each is a vapor, briefly substantial, ultimately empty. The diagnostic emptiness is therefore the great Old Testament wisdom verdict on the creature’s self-sufficient pursuit of meaning apart from its Creator: every pursuit, however richly stocked, ends in the same vapor. Doctrinally, however, the most surprising biblical emptiness is the kenosis of the Son of God in the incarnation. Philippians 2:7: Christ, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation (literally, emptied himself, heauton ekenosen), and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men. The Son did not cease to be God; the kenosis is not the emptying of the divine nature but the laying-aside of the independent use of divine prerogatives, the assumption of true humanity, the willingness to live the divine-human life under the conditions of the form of a servant, all the way to the death of the cross. The believer’s emptiness is a third register, derivative of the second. The saint, having seen the Son’s self-emptying, learns to empty himself of self-righteousness, self-trust, and self-aggrandizement, and to receive the fulness that the empty Christ has secured for the empty sinner. The Beatitude of the poor in spirit is this emptiness preceding fulness; the doctrine of justification by faith alone rests on the empty hand of faith that contributes nothing; the Christian life is the long discipline of being emptied of self that the soul may be more thoroughly filled with the fulness of Christ. The three emptinesses therefore stand in their proper relation: the diagnostic emptiness of every creature pursuit apart from God; the doctrinal self-emptying of the Son for our salvation; and the experiential emptying of the saint that conforms him, in measure, to the pattern of his Lord and prepares him to receive His fulness.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines EMPTINESS as the state of being empty; want of contents; vacuity; void space; figuratively, want of substance or solidity; want of value; in scripture, the vanity of created things apart from God (Ecclesiastes) and the self-emptying of Christ in the incarnation (Phil 2:7).
webster_full: EMPTINESS, n. — 1. A state of being empty; destitution of contents; vacuity; void space. 2. Want of substance or solidity; vanity; unsatisfactoriness. 3. Want of intellect or knowledge; vacuity of head; want of intelligence. 4. In scripture, the vanity (Heb. hebel, vapor) of created things considered apart from God, as in Ecclesiastes; and the kenosis of the Son in the incarnation (Phil 2:7).
scriptures: Ecclesiastes 1:2
Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.
Philippians 2:6-7
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men.
Matthew 5:3
Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Jeremiah 2:5
Thus saith the LORD, What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?
corruption_summary: Emptiness is corrupted, on the diagnostic side, by the affluent-distraction culture that has masked the Ecclesiastes verdict so successfully that whole lifetimes of meaningful pursuit can be lived without the soul ever facing it—and on the doctrinal side by the kenotic-Christology error that reads Phil 2:7 as Christ’s actual emptying of His divine attributes rather than the laying-aside of their independent use.
corruption_paragraphs: The affluent-distraction culture of the late-modern West has masked the Ecclesiastes verdict so successfully that whole lifetimes of meaningful-looking pursuit can be lived without the soul ever facing it. The Preacher’s diagnosis—that wealth, pleasure, wisdom, work, fame, and life itself considered apart from God are vapor—is fenced off from the contemporary believer’s daily experience by an endless supply of distractions, achievements, comforts, and stimulations that prevent the deep emptiness from being felt. The cure is partly providential (the providences that strip the masks: bereavement, failure, illness, the encounter with one’s mortality), partly disciplined (the deliberate silence, the fast, the prayer that lets the emptiness rise), and partly evangelistic (the gospel preached so that the emptiness, once felt, has the answer of the Christ who Himself was emptied to fill the empty). Recover the diagnostic emptiness, and the gospel recovers its addressees: the soul that has not faced its emptiness cannot receive the fulness Christ supplies.

The doctrinal corruption of the kenosis is the late-19th and 20th-century kenotic-Christology error, which reads Phil 2:7 as Christ’s actual emptying of His divine attributes (omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence) during the incarnation, so that the Christ of the Gospels is divinity-minus rather than divinity-veiled. The historic Reformed and Lutheran tradition has rejected this reading on several grounds: it contradicts the Chalcedonian definition (the two natures unconfused and unchanged); it leaves the church with a Christ who, during His earthly life, was not the One in whom all the fulness of the Godhead dwelt bodily (against Col 1:19; 2:9); and it makes the Son’s ongoing upholding of all things by the word of His power (Heb 1:3) impossible during the incarnation. The orthodox reading holds Phil 2:7 as the laying-aside of the independent use of divine prerogatives and the assumption of true humanity, not the laying-aside of deity itself. Recover both ends. The diagnostic emptiness opens the soul; the doctrinal self-emptying of the Son provides the answer; the believer’s emptiness empties him of self that he may be filled with the fulness of the Christ whose own self-emptying in the incarnation was, all the way through, the act of the Son who remained what He always was—true God and now also true man, full of grace and truth.
roots_summary: Hebrew hebel (vapor, breath, vanity—Ecclesiastes’ great word) and rīq (emptiness, vanity); Greek kenōsis-family from kenoō (to empty—Phil 2:7)—three biblical emptinesses: the diagnostic vapor of creature pursuit, the doctrinal self-emptying of the Son, and the experiential emptying of the saint.

Hebrew rīq (H7385) — emptiness, vanity.
Greek kenoō (G2758) — to empty (Phil 2:7).
Greek kenos (G2756) — empty, vain (1 Cor 15:14 of preaching vain if Christ be not risen).
usage: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity—the Ecclesiastes diagnostic on every creature pursuit apart from God.
Made himself of no reputation—the Son’s self-emptying in the incarnation is the laying-aside of the independent use of divine prerogatives, not the loss of deity.
Affluent-distraction culture masks the diagnostic emptiness; kenotic-Christology errors mistake the doctrinal one; biblical emptiness is the soil in which gospel fulness grows.

etymology: Old French tresor, from Latin thesaurus (treasure, storehouse), from Greek thēsauros. Renders the Hebrew ’ōtsār, “treasure, storehouse,” and segūllāh, “a peculiar treasure,” and the Greek thēsauros, “treasure, treasure-house.”
biblical_def: Treasure in Scripture is what the heart accounts most valuable—what is most carefully kept, most fondly returned to, most reluctantly parted with—and Christ Himself sets the diagnostic: for where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. The location of one’s actual treasure can be discovered by tracing the location of one’s actual heart, since the two are bound together. The Sermon on the Mount sets the two great treasure-options at maximum contrast: lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust doth corrupt, and where thieves do not break through nor steal. The earthly treasures are characterized by their vulnerability: moth eats, rust corrupts, thieves break through; they cannot be securely held. The heavenly treasures are characterized by their inviolability: nothing in heaven moths, rusts, or steals; what is laid up there cannot be lost. The application is therefore obvious in principle but searching in practice: where the saint deliberately invests his time, money, attention, and energy in the things of heaven (the gospel, the souls of men, the kingdom of Christ, the building up of the church, the relief of the poor, the unseen labors of prayer and faithfulness)—there his treasure is being laid up; and where the saint instead invests these same energies primarily in the things of earth (status, accumulation, comfort, leisure, the building of his own visible empire)—there his treasure remains exposed, and his heart with it. Scripture extends the treasure category in several beautiful ways. Israel is the LORD’s peculiar treasure (segūllāh)—a personal possession of distinct preciousness to the King of all the earth (Ex 19:5); the church inherits the title in 1 Pet 2:9 (a peculiar people). The treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid in Christ (Col 2:3); the gospel itself is the treasure carried in earthen vessels (2 Cor 4:7); the kingdom is the treasure hid in a field for which the man sold all that he had to buy the field (Matt 13:44); the saint is to be like the householder bringing forth out of his treasure things new and old (Matt 13:52). Treasure is therefore a category that organizes much of the Christian life: what the heart treasures, the soul becomes; where the treasure is laid up, the heart follows; what Christ counts as treasure becomes, by the regenerating Spirit, the very things the saint comes to treasure also.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TREASURE as wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve; great quantity of anything collected for future use; in scripture, that which is highly valued and carefully kept; spiritual riches.
webster_full: TREASURE, n. — 1. Wealth accumulated; particularly, a stock or store of money in reserve. 2. Great quantity of anything collected for future use. 3. Anything of much worth; that which is highly valued. For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also (Matt 6:21). 4. In scripture, that which is highly valued and carefully kept; spiritual riches; the gospel.
scriptures: Matthew 6:19-21

Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven... For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Matthew 13:44
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.
2 Corinthians 4:7
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
Colossians 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
corruption_summary: Treasure is corrupted by the materialist register of the present age that has trained the soul to treasure earthly things primarily and heavenly things vaguely—and by the inverse corruption of certain monastic and dualistic traditions that have denigrated created goods themselves as if they were the very things Scripture warns against treasuring.
corruption_paragraphs: The materialist register of late-modern consumer culture is the great contemporary corruption of treasure. The believer is trained from earliest life to identify the good life with accumulation: better house, better car, better retirement portfolio, better experiences, better resume. The very capacity to treasure heavenly things is atrophied by a culture that has reduced the imaginable goods to earthly ones. The diagnostic Christ gives is therefore searching: trace where the saint’s actual time, money, attention, and energy go, and you will find his actual treasure. If they go primarily into earthly accumulation and only marginally into the things of the kingdom, the heart is on earth no matter what the lips confess. The recovery is the deliberate redirection of those energies: time given to prayer and the Word, money given to the relief of the poor and the support of the gospel, attention given to the souls of men, energy given to the unseen labors of faithfulness—and the heart, by the law of treasure, follows.

The opposite corruption is the dualistic or monastic register that has denigrated created goods themselves as if they were the very things Scripture warns against treasuring. Christ does not condemn the having of wealth (Abraham had it, Joseph of Arimathea had it, Lydia had it); He warns against the laying-up of treasure on earth. The created goods—food, drink, beauty, marriage, family, work, play—are gifts of God to be received with thanksgiving, enjoyed in their proper place, and stewarded for the kingdom’s ends. They become treasures-in-the-corrupting-sense only when the heart fastens upon them as its ultimate good. The biblical balance is precise: enjoy God’s gifts as gifts; treasure the Giver and His kingdom as treasure; let the gifts serve the treasure and not displace it; hold the gifts with open hands and the treasure with the whole heart. The man whose hands are full of gifts and whose heart is full of God is the man Scripture commends—and the moth and rust and thief touch nothing he most loves.
roots_summary: Hebrew ’ōtsār (treasure, storehouse) and segūllāh (peculiar treasure); Greek thēsauros (treasure, treasure-house)—what the heart accounts most valuable; located by the trace of the heart’s actual investment; held secure when laid up in heaven where moth, rust, and thieves cannot reach it.
roots_lines: Hebrew ’ōtsār (H214) — treasure, storehouse.
Hebrew segūllāh (H5459) — peculiar treasure, personal possession (Ex 19:5; Deut 7:6; 14:2; 26:18; Mal 3:17).
Greek thēsauros (G2344) — treasure, treasure-house (Matt 6:19-21; 13:44; 2 Cor 4:7; Col 2:3).
Greek thēsaurizō (G2343) — to lay up treasure (Matt 6:19-20; 1 Cor 16:2; 2 Pet 3:7).
usage: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also—the diagnostic Christ gives for locating the heart’s actual loves.
Earthly treasure: moth, rust, thief. Heavenly treasure: none of these. The investment-recommendation is obvious in principle and searching in practice.
Materialism trains the soul to treasure earthly things; dualism denigrates created goods as such; biblical balance enjoys gifts as gifts and treasures the Giver as treasure.

etymology: From Old French regarder, “to look back, regard”; in later use, to repay or recompense. Renders the Hebrew sākār, “wages, reward,” and the Greek misthos, “wages, reward,” and antapodosis, “recompense.”
biblical_def: Reward in Scripture is the gracious recompense God promises and gives to those who diligently seek Him and serve Him faithfully—not earned wages owed to the worker but the free recompense of grace that rewards in the Father’s generosity the labor His own Spirit has wrought in His servants. The Hebrews 11 verse is foundational: but without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. The doctrine has structural weight in Christian discipleship. Christ Himself, in the Beatitudes, anchors the willingness to bear persecution in the assurance of reward: blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you... rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven. The Sermon on the Mount repeats the reward-motive across alms, prayer, and fasting (each time with the warning that to seek the reward of men’s recognition is to forfeit the reward of the Father). Paul speaks of his apostolic reward in 1 Cor 9: what is my reward then? Verily that, when I preach the gospel, I may make the gospel of Christ without charge. 2 John speaks of a full reward; Revelation 22:12 closes the Bible’s words with Christ’s own: and, behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be. The biblical doctrine of reward must be held in two precise balances. First, against works-righteousness: the reward is gracious recompense for what the Spirit has wrought in the saint, not wages earned by the saint as cause of his standing before God; justification is by faith alone in Christ alone, and rewards are a matter of differentiated grace among those already justified, not of standing. Second, against the false humility that refuses any motive of reward as somehow unworthy: Christ Himself motivates His disciples by it; Hebrews names God as the rewarder as the very content of faith; the apostles regularly appeal to reward; the saint is meant to be moved by it. The biblical pattern is therefore unselfconscious openness to the reward motive: the saint serves the Lord with the joy of knowing He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him, while resting all his standing before God on the imputed righteousness of Christ alone. The two together are the proper Christian disposition: assurance of standing in Christ, and joyful expectation of reward from the Father.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REWARD as recompense; remuneration; return for labor or services; in scripture, the recompense God gives to those who diligently seek Him and serve Him faithfully, not earned but graciously bestowed.
webster_full: REWARD, n. — 1. Recompense, or equivalent return for good done. 2. The fruit of men’s labor or works. Behold, his reward is with him (Isa 40:10). 3. Sum of money offered for any special service, as for the apprehension of a criminal. 4. In scripture, the recompense which God gives to those who diligently seek Him (Heb 11:6); the reward of grace (Rom 4:4).
scriptures: Hebrews 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Matthew 5:11-12
Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven.
1 Corinthians 3:14
If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward.
Revelation 22:12
And, behold, I come quickly; and my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be.
corruption_summary: The biblical doctrine of reward is corrupted, on one side, by the works-righteousness register that treats rewards as earned wages and confuses the basis of standing before God—and on the other by the false-humility register that refuses any reward motive as unworthy, against Christ’s own and the apostles’ explicit appeals.
corruption_paragraphs: The works-righteousness corruption confuses the basis of the saint’s standing before God. Rewards in Scripture are gracious recompense for what the Spirit has wrought in already-justified saints; they are not the means by which standing is secured. Where this distinction is collapsed, the doctrine of reward becomes a return to the law as the basis of acceptance, the saint’s assurance is shaken (because earned wages can be lost by failure), and the gospel itself is occluded. The Reformation precision is essential: justification by faith alone in Christ alone is the basis of standing; rewards are a matter of differentiated grace among those already justified, for service in which the Spirit Himself was the worker. Hold the two firmly, and the doctrine of reward keeps its motivational force without ever crossing into the moralism it has so often been confused with.

The opposite corruption is the false-humility register that refuses any reward motive as somehow unworthy of a true believer. The believer is told that he should serve God without any view to reward, that to be moved by promise of recompense is a lower spirituality, that the truly mature soul has transcended any such expectation. Christ Himself refuses this. He motivates His disciples by reward in the Beatitudes, in the Sermon on the Mount’s teaching on alms and prayer and fasting, in the parables of the talents and the faithful steward, in the closing words of the Bible (my reward is with me, to give every man according as his work shall be). The apostles regularly appeal to it. Hebrews names God as rewarder as the very content of faith. Recover both ends. Refuse the works-righteousness confusion that treats reward as the basis of standing, and refuse the false-humility refusal of the reward motive that Christ and the apostles uniformly employ. The biblical saint serves the Lord with joyful expectation of reward from a Father who delights to recompense the labor He Himself wrought in His servants—and rests all his standing meanwhile on the imputed righteousness of Christ alone.
roots_summary: Hebrew sākār (wages, reward); Greek misthos (wages, reward) and antapodosis (recompense)—the gracious recompense God gives to those who diligently seek Him, held in proper balance against works-righteousness on one side and false humility on the other.
roots_lines: Hebrew sākār (H7939) — wages, reward (Ps 127:3, children as a reward).
Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, reward (Matt 5:12; 6:1; 10:41-42; 1 Cor 3:8, 14; Heb 10:35; 2 John 8; Rev 22:12).
Greek antapodosis (G469) — recompense, repayment (Col 3:24).
Greek misthapodotēs (G3406) — rewarder (Heb 11:6, the rewarder of them that diligently seek him).
usage: He is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him—Hebrews 11:6 makes the doctrine of reward part of the content of saving faith.
Christ Himself motivates His disciples by reward; the false-humility refusal of the reward motive is unbiblical.
Works-righteousness treats reward as basis of standing; biblical doctrine holds standing in Christ alone and rewards as differentiated grace for Spirit-wrought labor.
